Higher interest rates can restrain inflation but weaken hiring; comparing the Fed’s policy cycle with labor-market conditions and Treasury yields reveals both this balancing act and its transmission across maturities.

![](/images/blog2/fed-balance-and-bond-maturities.png){fig-alt="Pastel hand-drawn illustration of a central bank balancing a grocery basket and a briefcase, with 2-, 10-, and 30-year Treasury bond characters."}

## From public pages to comparable data

I used `rvest` to extract yields from the [U.S. Treasury](https://home.treasury.gov/resource-center/data-chart-center/interest-rates/TextView?type=daily_treasury_yield_curve&field_tdr_date_value=2026), CPI and unemployment from the [Bureau of Labor Statistics](https://www.bls.gov/), and policy records from the [Federal Reserve](https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/openmarket.htm). Its key value is extracting dates and decision text from [FOMC statements](https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/fomccalendars.htm), allowing yield changes to be matched to the days policy news reaches markets.

CPI inflation is the seasonally adjusted index’s twelve-month percentage change. Each yield’s announcement-day change is its difference from the previous trading observation, multiplied by 100 to convert percentage points into **basis points**. The sample contains 1,178 Treasury dates, 56 macro months, and 18 rate-change announcements, ending in September 2026 for yields and August for macro data.

## The policy path and the dual mandate

The full schedule shows an unusually concentrated tightening phase, followed by a later easing cycle and the most recent increase.

::: {.table-scroll}
{{< include tables/policy_schedule.md >}}
:::

Four milestones make the macroeconomic sequence easier to see. Monthly values refer to the observation month, and the policy rate is the target-range midpoint then in effect.

{{< include tables/macro_milestones.md >}}

![Policy tightened after inflation surged, while unemployment stayed low. October 2025 CPI and unemployment observations are missing because of a lapse in appropriations.](/images/blog2/inflation_unemployment_with_events.png){fig-alt="Line chart of the federal funds target midpoint, year-over-year CPI inflation, and unemployment, with hike and cut markers."}

**The observed policy cycle is consistent with progress toward balancing inflation and employment, but not a completed or permanent success.** Inflation fell sharply without a large rise in unemployment, then rebounded. Four stages show how the balance changed:

- **Tightening, 2022–2023:** the policy midpoint rose above 5%. Inflation fell from its 9.0% peak to 3.3% by October 2023, while unemployment was 3.9%, close to its 4.0% starting level.
- **Holding high rates, 2023–2024:** by August 2024, inflation had fallen to 2.6%, while unemployment reached 4.2%. Further disinflation coincided with a softer labor market.
- **Easing, 2024–2025:** inflation generally stayed around 2.5–3%, while unemployment reached 4.4% in September 2025. The shift toward cuts was consistent with greater concern about employment.
- **Renewed tightening, 2026:** inflation reached 4.2% in May and eased to 3.4% in August, with unemployment at 4.1%. Renewed price pressure provides context for September’s hike; its macroeconomic effects are outside this sample.

These patterns cannot isolate policy’s causal contribution. CPI tracks price pressure here; the Fed’s formal inflation goal uses PCE prices.

## Three maturities, one policy cycle

The yield summary compares January 3, 2022 with September 18, 2026; peaks are sample highs.

{{< include tables/yield_levels.md >}}

![Daily 2-year, 10-year, and 30-year Treasury yields with Fed rate-change announcements.](/images/blog2/daily_yields_with_events.png){fig-alt="Three Treasury yield curves over time with vertical markers for Fed hikes and cuts."}

**Treasury yields did not move uniformly across maturities: the short end reversed more visibly with the policy cycle, while long yields remained elevated.** The 2-year yield peaked at 5.19% in 2023, above longer maturities. By October 2024, the 30-year again exceeded the 10-year and 2-year. During 2025, the 30-minus-2-year gap widened from 0.61 percentage points in January to 1.07 in October as shorter yields fell more. By September 2026, 10- and 30-year yields were still 5.01% and 5.34%, showing that earlier cuts had not ensured lasting relief in long-term financing costs.

The announcement-day distribution makes that maturity contrast more direct.

{{< include tables/yield_responses.md >}}

![Absolute announcement-day Treasury yield changes by maturity.](/images/blog2/announcement_day_yield_changes.png){fig-alt="Boxplots and points showing larger absolute announcement-day moves for the 2-year yield than for 10-year and 30-year yields."}

**Announcement-day movements were larger at shorter maturities:** median absolute changes were 7.0, 5.0, and 2.5 basis points for 2-, 10-, and 30-year yields. The 2-year yield is more closely tied to near-term policy expectations; longer yields also incorporate distant rates and compensation for long-term risk. This provides an interpretation of the maturity pattern, not proof that each announced decision caused the daily move. The sample includes only rate-changing meetings, and daily changes also contain other news.

## So, did the Fed pull it off?

**The evidence suggests progress in balancing inflation and employment, alongside stronger announcement-day yield movements at shorter maturities.** Inflation’s rebound shows why that balance requires reassessment rather than declaring victory after disinflation. For investors, the practical implication is to distinguish near-term yield sensitivity from long-bond price risk: smaller yield moves do not necessarily mean smaller price losses, because longer-duration bonds are more sensitive to a given yield change. For borrowers, a Fed cut alone is insufficient evidence that long-term financing has become cheaper; the relevant maturity’s market yield still matters.
